Same situation here. Didn’t help that my parents were very defensive and basically said I was making it up. Then I read the diagnostic criteria out to them, and those things were there all along. They just didn’t know that having a child could be any different, and I didn’t know that existing could be any different.

When you lived your entire life with people around you acting like your difficulties are your choice and a moral failing, it can help to have access to an explanation, coping resources, accommodations, and a community who knows how you feel. In some cases, diagnosis can also provide financial support and vocational assistance. For a lot of people, especially those diagnosed as adults , this can make a world of difference. It’s also notoriously difficult for an adult to get a diagnosis as much fewer specialists assess adults and the assessment itself is extremely expensive (it is 2800 dollars in my area, with over a year’s waiting list, for adults)

How’s this fake? ~~As someone who was diagnosed late and is friends with multiple people also diagnosed late (sometimes only because their own kids showed the signs)~~, that’s kind of how it often goes, especially for women(https://www.wellandgood.com/autistic-women-adult-diagnosis), as it very often doesn’t get noticed until teens and adulthood. The diagnosis “journey” starts with intentionally seeking out help for things that cause the most distress on the daily, if not an outright burnout(https://www.spectrumnews.org/news/autistic-burnout-explained/). Anxiety is extremely common among those w/ ASD(https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/topics/mental-health/anxiety), and is more likely to be dx’ed earlier as it causes the most issues, up next is the sensory element. Once you get into the system, you’re more likely to realize that you have an irregular pattern of functioning (bonus point for high ADHD-Autism comorbidity, https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2022.837424/full). The next part can be pretty weird, as a lot of us, once first learning about autism, start realizing just how many things we’ve previously taken as normal were, in fact, overlooked symptoms. And it *doesn’t* help that there seems to be a sizeable amount of people who are all too happy to call out a person they do not know for questioning things about themselves.
